report:
The evidence does not support a clear "yes" — the overall conclusion is that ginkgo biloba extract has not been reliably shown to relieve tinnitus.

The most rigorous synthesis, a Cochrane systematic review (four RCTs, 1,543 participants), found "the limited evidence does not demonstrate that Ginkgo biloba is effective for tinnitus" and rated certainty of evidence as low, with no clear benefit on tinnitus loudness, intrusiveness, or quality of life (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/; https://www.cochrane.org/hr/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus).

Individual trial results are inconsistent. A large randomized, placebo-controlled trial by Rejali et al. and a subsequent meta-analysis concluded "Ginkgo biloba does not benefit patients with tinnitus" (https://www.tinnitusjournal.com/articles/ginkgo-biloba-in-the-treatment-of-tinnitus-an-updated-literature-review.html). However, other studies using the specific standardized extract EGb 761® at higher doses (120 mg twice daily) have shown modest symptom improvement, and some authors argue EGb 761® specifically may be an "evidence-based treatment option," while other ginkgo formulations lack proven efficacy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/).

Overall, methodological quality varies widely across studies (differing doses, formulations, and outcome measures), which likely explains the conflicting results. The most authoritative, independent review (Cochrane) concludes there is insufficient reliable evidence that ginkgo relieves tinnitus.

**Conclusion:** The evidence is mixed and generally weak. Ginkgo biloba, including the well-studied EGb 761® formulation, may show benefit in some individual trials, but the highest-quality systematic evidence (Cochrane) does not confirm effectiveness for tinnitus relief. The answer is likely "no" or "unproven" rather than a confident "yes."
